extracted.intended_audience: researchers, research-integrity professionals, journal editors, scientific sleuths, and science journalists
extracted.subtask_description: A collection of news items and case examples documenting image manipulation, duplication, AI alteration, and related research-integrity failures in biomedical and related fields; useful for understanding what kinds of image issues trigger corrections, expressions of concern, retractions, investigations, and legal action. The page illustrates real-world examples and consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: repeating patterns in electron microscopy data
rubrics_metrics.description: The paper 'contained repeating patterns in the electron microscopy data.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Royal Society of Chemistry found repeating patterns in EM images which contributed to a paper's retraction; repeating patterns in microscopy images are a red flag for manipulation or inappropriate reuse of image regions.

rubrics_metrics.name: identical cell images across publications (duplicate images)
rubrics_metrics.description: Images depicting cells that were identical to those included in a later paper with a number of the same authors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: identical cell images appearing in different papers (even by the same authors) prompted retraction. Duplicate images across publications can indicate improper reuse, self-plagiarism, or fabrication and are grounds for corrective action.

rubrics_metrics.name: AI-manipulated imagery / superimposed elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors acknowledged having used AI to superimpose the tape ruler in the figure (clinical image).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: NEJM retracted a short clinical-image piece after authors admitted AI was used to alter the photo. AI-based alterations (superimposing measurement tools or other elements) are not acceptable if not disclosed and can lead to retraction and media attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: overlapping images / image overlaps / duplications
rubrics_metrics.description: Papers containing overlapping images, image overlaps, or duplications across figures or manuscripts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple journals flagged and retracted papers for overlapping images and duplications. Overlaps may be detected across figures within one paper or between different papers and are commonly cited in expressions of concern, corrections, or retractions.

rubrics_metrics.name: inappropriate editing of micrographs
rubrics_metrics.description: Instances of 'inappropriate editing' of micrographs reported in retraction notices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the International Journal of Molecular Science retracted papers for duplications and 'inappropriate editing' of micrographs. Editing that alters scientific meaning or fabricates results is misconduct; careful examination of raw micrographs is needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: data/images appearing in an earlier publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Figures or data that 'appeared in an earlier publication.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a paper was retracted for containing data that appeared in an earlier publication. Reusing previously published data/images without proper citation or justification, or presenting them as new, can trigger retraction for duplication or plagiarism.

rubrics_metrics.name: falsification during figure creation
rubrics_metrics.description: Falsification occurred during creation of a figure (e.g., 'falsification occurred during creation of figure S9C').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: institutional misconduct investigations found falsification in figure creation and requested retraction. Falsification of figures (manipulating data to change results) is a core form of research misconduct and usually prompts institutional action and retraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: manipulating images in grant updates and reporting fabricated results
rubrics_metrics.description: Manipulating images in grant updates and reporting the fabricated results in research performance progress reports.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: ORI sanctioned a researcher for intentionally falsifying images in an unpublished manuscript and in two grant updates and for reporting fabricated results in progress reports. Image manipulation in grant-related documents is subject to federal oversight and sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: misrepresented and/or duplicated images supporting grant applications (legal/financial consequences)
rubrics_metrics.description: Images and data that were 'misrepresented and/or duplicated' in support of grant applications to the NIH.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Dana-Farber settled a False Claims Act suit, admitting images/data were misrepresented and/or duplicated in grant applications, leading to a $15 million settlement. Misrepresentation of images in funding applications can carry legal and financial liability.

rubrics_metrics.name: fabricated allegations of image manipulation (verification anti-pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: Anonymous allegations that include manipulated/enlarged images that themselves are fabricated and do not match the original images.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a PubPeer anonymous comment alleged duplication, but closer inspection showed the commenter had fabricated enlarged images; original showed two different lanes. This warns that allegations should be verified against originals, as some allegations can be faked.

rubrics_metrics.name: copy-and-paste lane duplication (specific manipulation technique)
rubrics_metrics.description: A single lane had been copied and pasted on top of an adjacent lane in a western blot image.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: experts identified a copied-and-pasted lane as the method used to fake a duplication. Recognizing specific manipulation techniques (copy-paste, cloning, rotation, stretching) aids detection and assessment of image integrity.
